clips.end_words: Ascorbic acid is not vitamin C
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau tells the story of why British sailors were once nicknamed "limeys."

Sailors used to come down with scurvy on long voyages, until the British navy started handing out limes, lemons and other citrus. The vitamin C in the fruit stopped it cold.

His point: that same fix doesn't work with ascorbic acid, the lab-made ingredient most labels simply call "vitamin C." Give someone with scurvy ascorbic acid, he says, and it does nothing; real citrus does.

Is the vitamin C on your label the real thing?

#kevintrudeau #vitaminc #supplements #healthtruth #readthelabel #wellness

Kevin Trudeau tells the story of a B vitamin that got quietly swapped for something else: niacin.

Real niacin can cause a "niacin flush," a brief red, hot, itchy feeling some people find uncomfortable, even though it passes in minutes. So, in Kevin Trudeau's telling, manufacturers had chemists create niacinamide, a related compound that skips the flush, and started labeling it as niacin anyway.

His point: niacinamide is not niacin, even with government sign-off to call it that on a label.

His advice: if you see "niacin (niacinamide)" on a bottle, put it back on the shelf.

#kevintrudeau #niacin #vitamins #healthtruth #readthelabel #wellness

Kevin Trudeau uses a kitchen example to explain why a supplement's ingredient ratio matters as much as the ingredients themselves.

Picture a soup recipe gone wrong: half a cup of water, but 45 chicken bones and 50 bay leaves. Every ingredient on its own is fine; the proportions make it inedible.

His point: food and supplements work the same way. Nutrients have to arrive in roughly the proportions nature built into real food, not whatever ratio is cheapest to manufacture.

What's the ratio on the supplement in your own cabinet?
